title: Monday in the Sun
full_review:
Five laid-off dock workers struggle to maintain their dignity while looking for employment in the complex character study "Mondays in the Sun" (Lions Gate).

Spanish director Fernando Leon de Aranoa has beautifully captured the essence of the delicate connection between the male ego and worthy employment. As these men cling to each other's friendship for support and affirmation of their own value, it is clear how much their identity is wrapped up in their ability to find a job. Leon also makes a statement about the futility of the Spanish government employment offices, which instead of helping the unemployed only add to their embarrassment and desperation.

The Spanish film has its own comfortable tempo which reflects the pace of the men's lives. Santa (Javier Bardem, many pounds heavier and sporting a grizzled beard), insecure Jose (Luis Tosar), sweaty-palmed Lino (Jose Angel Egid), Russian Sergei (Serge Riaboukine) and the aging Amador (Celso Bugallo) sit around their pal Rico's (Joaquin Climent) bar, drinking more than they can pay for, philosophizing or just plain shooting the breeze. All have been booted from their jobs on the shipyard in Vigo in northern Spain. And although Rico has moved on, the rest are sad sacks trying to make the ends of a very short string meet.

Santa spends his day picking up women, such as Angela (Laura Dominquez), a cheese girl in the local supermarket, and taking baby-sitting jobs from Rico's 15-year-old daughter, Nata (Aida Folch). In a telling scene, Santa is reading the story of the fun-loving grasshopper and the dutiful ant to his charge when he explodes, unable to contain himself, fuming over the self-righteousness of the ant and the plight of the poor, unfortunate souls who are born grasshoppers. His tragicomic reaction to the story is the key to unlocking the narrative's core.

The story moves along revealing how each character's personality has been affected by his job loss. Jose has become jealous of his beautiful wife, Ana (Nieve de Medina), who douses herself in perfume when she comes back from her job at a tuna-packing plant. He's afraid that his joblessness makes him less of a man in her eyes. Lino worries about his advancing age, furtively dyeing his gray hair and stealing his teen-age son's clothes in order to compete with younger men in job interviews. And Amador has become increasingly distant and enraged since his wife left to supposedly visit her sickly mother. His days are spent nursing his wounds with alcohol.

Santa is the center of the story, and he also holds the gang together. Although they may find him abrasive and bitter, the men still gravitate toward him as a means of strength and direction. It is through him that the audience most fully experiences the emotions of a proud man forced to face his limitations.

"Mondays in the Sun" is an affecting slice-of-life film that offers a sensitive perspective on the macho world.

Subtitles.

Because of an implied sexual encounter and much rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
